newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Alphabet soup puzzles old and new at WTO meeting.
newsitem.headline: Alphabet soup puzzles old and new at WTO meeting.

text.p: If you think GRULA and cabotage are types of soup, a new glossary published in Singapore this week could help.

Given to the more than 1,000 journalists at the five-day inaugural ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO), which began on Monday, the mini-dictionary includes dozens of strange terms and acronyms from the arcane world of international trade.
"Even old hands sometimes get confused with all the terms," one Singaporean official distributing the glossary told Reuters.
"There are so many of them," added the official, who declined to be identified.
The new guide attempts to outline most of the key terms used by the WTO officials, who have assembled in Singapore from the WTO's 128 member-states.
It details some of the hundreds of international agreements signed by WTO members as a group and in smaller regional groupings over the last century.

These are so numerous that a brief Reuters survey of diplomats at the WTO on Monday produced no consensus on the difference between, or content of, a range of pacts covering intellectual property rights.

Not one of the officials quizzed could tell the difference between the Lisbon Agreement, the Madrid Agreement, the Paris Convention, the Rome Convention or the Washington Treaty, all of which are listed in the new glossary.
"I have no idea what these are," said a Canadian diplomat.
Queries over the meaning of GRULA, an informal group of Latin American members of the WTO, received a similar response.
"It sounds like a soup," the Canadian diplomat said.
A British diplomat, who requested anonymity, confessed he also had no idea what GRULA was, but thought "cabotage" had something to do with air traffic.
The term refers to sea shipping between ports of the same country, usually along coasts.
The nine-page learners' lexicon comes in particularly useful when listening to discussions over agricultural policy, which is occupying the minds of a large proportion of the delegates.
It even explains briefly Europe's CAP, or Common Agricultural Policy, which has resulted in huge "butter mountains" and "wine lakes" since it was introduced to support the region's farmers.

Much of the glossary is concerned with lists of acronyms for regional groupings and with ungainly extension of words such as "tariffication", which refers to procedures relating to agricultural market access.
In the trade context, even apparently normal words have complex and hidden meanings.

At the WTO, "swing" is the transfer of one part of a quota from one product to another and a "conference" is a group of container lines in maritime transport "which have anti-trust immunity for the purpose of collectively setting rates".
"You're joking," said a Dutch diplomat, as this was explained.
"Why haven't we been given this?"
